hero.title: Eight steps from a first look to finished homes
hero.lede: The eight steps a Colorado affordable rental or for-sale project goes through, from choosing a community to leasing or selling the homes, with the public data source for each step and what that data cannot tell you.

stat_strip.label: Colorado housing shortfall
stat_strip.sub: Estimated statewide shortfall of homes in 2023, at all income levels, down from about 140,000 at its 2019 peak.
stat_strip.source: Colorado State Demography Office, housing shortfall analysis released September 17, 2025 (2023 estimate).

stat_strip.label: Pipeline stages
stat_strip.sub: Each stage ends in a concrete next move, with confidence and limits to keep in mind.

stat_strip.label: Readiness categories
stat_strip.sub: A neutral way to describe where a community may be in its own affordable-housing planning cycle.

intro.why_this_matters: The State Demography Office's shortfall figure above has eased since 2019, but affordability has gotten worse. Each step below asks a narrower question: where is need documented, can the local market support new homes, and is a project likely to get built. The sources are ACS, HUD CHAS, CHFA and DOLA, and every step names its own.
how_to_read: Each stage is sequential. Stage 1 narrows the universe; Stage 8 ends with a concrete action.
Every stage lists its data source, a confidence rating (high / medium / low), the limits to keep in mind, and what the stage does NOT tell you.
Jargon is defined inline the first time it appears — hover or tap any underlined term for a plain-English definition.
This page is a public-data reference for anyone reading along; it does not include specific sites, owner names, or relationship status.

ami_anchor.title: What AMI actually means in dollars
ami_anchor.preface: Affordable housing programs use percentages of AMI to set who qualifies and what rents are allowed. Here is what those percentages translate to in dollars for a household of four in three representative Colorado counties — to make the bands concrete.
ami_anchor.footnote: AMI bands matter because LIHTC and most state programs target the 30-60% range, where renters typically cannot pay market rents and the gap is widest. Households at 80-120% (workforce) are the focus of Colorado's MIHTC and Prop 123 programs. Above 120% generally pays market rent.

steps.title: Jurisdiction Screen
steps.summary: Reduce 64 counties, 272 municipalities and Colorado's Census Designated Places to a workable short list using population-weighted housing-need indicators.
steps.what_this_means: The starting universe is all 64 Colorado counties, the state's 272 incorporated municipalities (cities and towns), and its Census Designated Places, the unincorporated communities the Census Bureau reports separately. The Jurisdiction Screen reduces that universe to a short list where housing need, market conditions, and policy posture line up well enough to justify a closer look. A jurisdiction here means a county or place with its own Census GEOID — the standard federal identifier used to keep data joined cleanly across sources.
steps.why_it_matters: A first screen keeps attention on the places where need is concentrated. Population-weighted need indicators point to communities where new affordable homes would serve the most households earning 30-80% of area median income (AMI).

data_sources.label: ACS 5-year
data_sources.what: Population, median income, tenure, rent, vacancy

data_sources.label: HUD income limits & FMRs
data_sources.what: Affordability benchmark by county / metro

data_sources.label: CHFA LIHTC inventory
data_sources.what: Existing affordable supply by place

data_sources.label: CHAS-derived place-level AMI gap
data_sources.what: Demand vs. supply at each income band

steps.confidence_note: Inputs are authoritative federal datasets, but each carries its own vintage and methodology assumptions. Verify local figures with the planning director or housing authority before treating any single number as decisive.
watch_outs: Small-place ACS estimates carry wide margins of error — cross-check against county totals before acting on a single number.
Resort and college-town economies distort median income upward — a high median can mask deep cost-burden for the local workforce.
A jurisdiction with low absolute need but a fast-growing employment base can still belong on the short list.
steps.does_not_tell_you: Whether a specific parcel is buildable, whether the council will support a project, or whether the housing authority has capacity to operate new units.
steps.next_step: Short-listed jurisdictions move into Stage 2 for a data-quality check before any qualitative work begins.

steps.title: QA/QC Check
steps.summary: Verify the underlying data is current, complete, and reconciles across sources before any conclusion is drawn.
steps.what_this_means: QA/QC — Quality Assurance / Quality Control — is the discipline of verifying that the numbers being used are current, complete, and internally consistent. Before drawing any conclusion from a jurisdiction screen, the underlying datasets should be run through a freshness audit, a coverage audit, and a reconciliation check against external sources.
steps.why_it_matters: Out-of-date or incomplete data gives precise-looking wrong answers. A tax-credit inventory missing a recent 80-unit lease-up will overstate need. An ACS vintage older than the latest income limits will understate the gap. Catching these mismatches here keeps them out of a site recommendation later.
steps.why_a_council_member_should_care: If a council member is asked to commit local money or zoning capacity to a project, they should know whether the need figure is current, what its margin of error is, and how it compares with the State Demography Office and HUD CHAS figures. Stage 2 is where those three answers are written down.

external_reconciliation.title: Three external sources to reconcile against before relying on a number

sources.name: BLS QCEW
sources.purpose: Quarterly employment and wage data, county-level

external_reconciliation.note: When the three sources disagree by more than 10%, report the range, not a single number.

data_sources.label: Data Health page
data_sources.what: A page on the site (Data Health, linked from the footer) shows the freshness status of every dataset on the site. For each one it lists when the original source was published, when the local copy was last refreshed, how complete the coverage is, and whether it's current or stale. If something is overdue, a red badge shows up. Before anyone quotes a number from this site in an investment memo or council pitch, they can check this page in 10 seconds to confirm the underlying data is current.

data_sources.label: File fingerprinting
data_sources.what: Every data file gets a fingerprint each night. If a government source updates a file in place, with the same filename and new numbers, the fingerprint changes and the change is flagged. HUD and CHFA do this a few times a year.

data_sources.label: Cross-checks against independent sources
data_sources.what: Before any housing-need or projection figure is relied on, it should be cross-checked against three independent sources: (1) the state's own population projections from the Colorado Demography Office, (2) jobs data from the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics, and (3) the federal cost-burden survey from HUD. If all three external sources roughly agree but a local number disagrees, that's a flag — the methodology is worth a second look. If the three sources themselves disagree (common in small Colorado towns where the underlying surveys have wide margins of error), publish the range instead of one number.

steps.confidence_note: High for federally administered sources (ACS, HUD, Census TIGER). Medium for state inventories that depend on developer self-reporting (LIHTC placed-in-service updates can lag by a quarter or two).
watch_outs: Different ACS vintages can disagree by 5-10% in small places — report the range, not just the point estimate.
Geographic boundaries change: a 2020 Census tract may have been split since, and joins to older data need to be redone, not assumed.
HUD income limits update every spring; running an analysis in March against last year's limits will read as a larger gap than truly exists.
CHFA's published LIHTC inventory can lag actual placements-in-service by 1-4 quarters — stamp every CHFA figure with its inventory generation date.
steps.does_not_tell_you: Whether the data is right for any specific block or building — only that it passes baseline freshness, coverage, and reconciliation checks.
steps.next_step: Once datasets pass QA/QC for the jurisdictions on the short list, the analysis can be trusted enough to test against on-the-ground reality in Stage 3.

steps.title: Local Verification
steps.summary: Confirm that what the data shows is still true on the ground — read minutes, plans, and talk to local staff.
steps.what_this_means: Local Verification confirms that what the data says is still true on the ground today. This is where recent council minutes, comprehensive plans, housing strategies, and capital improvement plans for the jurisdictions on the short list are read carefully — and where the housing authorities, advocacy groups, and planning departments expected to be there are confirmed as still active.
steps.why_it_matters: Federal tables lag by a year or more. A jurisdiction that adopted an inclusionary housing policy three months ago, paused a fee waiver program last quarter, or approved a 200-unit project last week will not show those changes in any ACS or HUD table for at least a year. Reading minutes and calling staff closes that gap.
steps.community_engagement_note: This step also includes talking with community organizations, advocacy groups, and residents directly whenever proximity allows. Public data shows where need exists; local conversations show what the community wants the response to look like.

data_sources.label: Local-resources directory
data_sources.what: Housing authorities, nonprofits, and planning offices by place

data_sources.label: Municipal websites
data_sources.what: Comprehensive plans, housing strategies, council agendas

data_sources.label: Council & planning-commission minutes
data_sources.what: Recent policy moves, project approvals, fee changes

steps.confidence_note: The directory is high-confidence (continuously maintained, with roughly 185 links re-verified in the most recent audit). The underlying policy facts evolve weekly — any specific claim should be re-checked before being used in a funding application.
watch_outs: A jurisdiction's website often lags its own decisions — a current ordinance may not be posted for weeks after adoption.
Volunteer or part-time planning staff in smaller jurisdictions means a non-response is not a no.
Housing-strategy plans frequently set goals without committing funding — record both the goal and the funding mechanism, separately.
steps.does_not_tell_you: Whether a specific council member or staff person will support a specific project. That requires direct conversation, not document review.
steps.next_step: Verified jurisdictions are then assessed for partnership readiness in Stage 4.

steps.title: Partnership Readiness Assessment
steps.summary: Group communities by where each one is in its own affordable housing planning, so a developer, funder or advocate knows what kind of help fits.
steps.what_this_means: Where a community is in its planning shows in its adopted plans, current funding and recent CHFA activity. The four tiers match a partner's help to that readiness. They are a planning tool, not a public ranking of communities.

buckets.name: In Active Partnership
buckets.definition: The community is in active conversations with development partners right now. Adopted plans, available funding tools, and CHFA history all point to a window where a project can come together in the near term.

buckets.name: Building Together
buckets.definition: Strong housing need is documented and the community is building policy capacity. Conversations are underway about the steps that would make a project possible, typically dedicated local funding, an updated land-use code, or more staff.

buckets.name: Long-Horizon Conversation
buckets.definition: Real housing need is documented, but the policies that support near-term construction are still being written. Useful help here is technical assistance on the adopted plan and staying in touch until the community is ready.

buckets.name: Future Partner
buckets.definition: The timing is not right for a near-term project, sometimes because the community has chosen a different path and sometimes because of water, wastewater or terrain limits. The community's adopted direction is respected, and a later conversation stays possible if priorities change.

steps.why_it_matters: Developers and funders do best when they arrive at the right time. The four tiers point attention to communities where a project can close in the current funding cycle. A community in the long-horizon tier today can move up after a comprehensive plan update, and the tiers make that easier to see coming.

data_sources.label: Synthesis of Stages 1-3
data_sources.what: AMI gap magnitude, ACS context, CHFA inventory, civic-capacity scorecard, local verification notes

steps.confidence_note: Inputs are high-confidence; the synthesis is a judgment call. Reclassification typically happens quarterly, with reasons for any movement between buckets documented so others can read and challenge the call.
watch_outs: A high score on the civic-capacity scorecard reflects policy adoption, not policy implementation — a jurisdiction can have an inclusionary ordinance on the books and no projects yet built under it.
Election cycles can shift a jurisdiction one bucket in either direction within a single quarter.
The bucket is the jurisdiction's, not the project's. A great site in a C jurisdiction is still a great site.
steps.does_not_tell_you: Which jurisdictions specifically fall into each category today. Public reference pages should describe the criteria without publishing current classifications for named communities.
steps.next_step: A and B jurisdictions move into site strategy in Stage 5; C and D jurisdictions remain on a monitoring list with quarterly review.

steps.title: Site Strategy
steps.summary: Work through eight site-type lenses in order — from easiest path (public land) to hardest (annexation).
steps.what_this_means: Site strategy is the question of where, within a chosen jurisdiction, an affordable project can actually be built. Eight site-type lenses are worth working through in roughly this order — moving from the easiest path to the hardest.

lenses.label: City-owned land
lenses.note: Surplus municipal parcels, often already studied in a published land inventory.

lenses.label: County-owned land
lenses.note: Similar to city parcels but typically larger and further from existing infrastructure.

lenses.label: School-district land
lenses.note: Underused district parcels, increasingly paired with workforce-housing partnerships for teachers and staff.

lenses.label: Church and faith-community land
lenses.note: Parking lots, parsonages, and underbuilt campuses, often available on a long-term ground lease.

lenses.label: Institutional land
lenses.note: Hospitals, universities, and anchor institutions with land they no longer need at full operational scale.

lenses.label: Large vacant parcels
lenses.note: Privately owned undeveloped land at sizes that support meaningful unit counts, typically inside the urban services boundary.

lenses.label: Underutilized commercial sites
lenses.note: Aging strip centers, oversized parking fields, obsolete office parks suitable for redevelopment or adaptive reuse.

lenses.label: Annexation candidates
lenses.note: Adjacent unincorporated land that could be brought into the jurisdiction to enable utility extension — the longest path.

steps.why_it_matters: Land cost and entitlement are the two biggest reasons an affordable project does or does not pencil. Working the eight lenses in order puts the fastest paths first and leaves the harder ones for places where the easier ones are used up.

data_sources.label: Municipal land inventories
data_sources.what: Surplus city/county parcels with stated housing intent

data_sources.label: County assessor records
data_sources.what: Ownership, acreage, land-use code

data_sources.label: Census TIGER boundaries
data_sources.what: Jurisdictional context

data_sources.label: Comprehensive plans
data_sources.what: Future land-use categories, urban services boundaries

steps.confidence_note: Public parcel data is reliable for ownership and acreage. Current development feasibility — utilities at the curb, environmental conditions, easements — requires site-specific diligence no public dataset can substitute for.
watch_outs: 'Vacant' in the assessor's database can mean 'no building' rather than 'developable' — wetlands, floodway, and steep slope are common surprises.
Institutional landowners often have internal real-estate processes that take 12-18 months independent of any developer's timeline.
Annexation requires both jurisdictional willingness and a contiguous boundary — without contiguity, the path is foreclosed regardless of policy posture.
steps.does_not_tell_you: Whether a specific owner is willing to sell or ground-lease. That always requires a direct conversation.
steps.next_step: A short list of viable site lenses for the jurisdiction feeds the readiness review in Stage 6.

steps.title: Financing Readiness — LIHTC rental and affordable ownership
steps.summary: Assess each jurisdiction-site pairing against five readiness levels — on whichever track the project is on: tax-credit rental or restricted ownership. The two tracks share the questions up to here; this is where they diverge, and where the obligations that follow closing differ most.
steps.what_this_means: Up to this step the path is the same for any project: where, who needs what, does the market support it, does the deal pencil. From here, two conventional financing tracks split. The federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC), administered in Colorado by CHFA, supplies equity for most new affordable rental construction — projects compete for 9% credits (competitive, scored annually) or 4% credits (paired with tax-exempt bonds, available on a rolling basis subject to a state allocation cap). Affordable ownership — deed-restricted for-sale homes, community land trusts, shared-equity models — is financed instead with down-payment assistance, soft second mortgages, land held by a trust, and buyer mortgages, and keeps the home affordable at resale rather than at rent. Each track has its own five readiness levels below, and its own obligations after closing.
steps.readiness_label: LIHTC rental — the five readiness levels

readiness_levels.name: Conceptual
readiness_levels.definition: Need is documented and the jurisdiction is in the A or B bucket, but no specific site, sponsor, or financing structure is identified yet.

readiness_levels.name: Site identified
readiness_levels.definition: A specific parcel is in view, with confirmed zoning, basic utility availability, and preliminary acreage and yield estimates.

readiness_levels.name: Pre-application
readiness_levels.definition: A development team and sponsor are organized, a preliminary unit mix and AMI targeting are set, and a market study or HNA supports the rent structure.

readiness_levels.name: Application ready
readiness_levels.definition: Site control is in place (option, contract, or letter of intent), a full financing stack is assembled in concept, environmental and design work has started, and local approvals are in process.

readiness_levels.name: Funded
readiness_levels.definition: CHFA has reserved credits, the financing stack is closed or near closing, and the project is moving toward construction start.

ownership_track.title: Affordable ownership — the five readiness levels
ownership_track.what_this_means: Deed-restricted for-sale homes, community land trust (CLT) homes, and shared-equity models sell to income-qualified buyers at a below-market price and stay affordable through a resale formula, not a rent restriction. The same five-level shape applies, but the milestones are about the buyer pool, the subsidy per home, and the resale convention rather than a credit award. The levels mirror the site's ownership decision chain: site and price context, demand by price band, per-unit subsidy gap, developer funding stack, resale convention.

readiness_levels.name: Conceptual
readiness_levels.definition: Ownership need is documented (income-qualified households who could carry a mortgage at a restricted price, but not at market) and the jurisdiction is in the A or B bucket; no site, sponsor, or stewardship entity is identified yet.

readiness_levels.name: Site and price band identified
readiness_levels.definition: A parcel is in view with zoning that allows for-sale product, and the demand-by-price-band screen shows enough qualified buyers at the target restricted price — not just enough renters.

readiness_levels.name: Subsidy gap sized
readiness_levels.definition: The per-home gap between total development cost and the restricted sale price is quantified, and the sources that would fill it (down-payment assistance, soft seconds, land contribution, Prop 123 or local funds) are named in concept.

readiness_levels.name: Stewardship and resale convention set
readiness_levels.definition: A stewardship entity (CLT, housing authority, or program administrator) is committed, the resale formula is chosen (fixed cap, shared appreciation, or index-based), and the deed restriction or ground lease is drafted. Site control is in place and buyer-financing lenders who will underwrite restricted homes are identified.

readiness_levels.name: Funded and enrolled
readiness_levels.definition: Gap sources are committed, the restriction is recorded or ready to record, the buyer-qualification process is set up, and construction or acquisition is moving toward start.

watch_outs: A restricted price only works if buyers can get a mortgage on a restricted home — check that at least one lender will underwrite the deed restriction or ground lease before counting on the buyer pool.
Stewardship is a decades-long commitment; a resale formula with no entity to enforce it lapses at the first sale.
Ownership need and rental need are not the same households — a jurisdiction with acute renter cost burden can still have a thin qualified-buyer pool at the target price.
ownership_track.does_not_tell_you: Which resale convention a jurisdiction will accept, or how long the restriction will hold — those are local policy and legal choices the ownership decision chain surfaces but cannot decide.

after_closing.label: What follows closing — the obligations each track carries
after_closing.intro: Closing starts a new set of obligations. Both tracks carry ongoing reporting, certification and long-term obligations, and they differ in kind. These are the ones a first-time sponsor most often learns about late.

obligations.what: Placed-in-service documentation and first-year credit claim (IRS Form 8609 for each building)
obligations.when: At placed-in-service and the first credit year
obligations.if_missed: Credits cannot be claimed for the year; investor equity installments are typically conditioned on it

obligations.what: Tenant income certification at move-in and annual recertification; rent held at or below the AMI-tier ceiling
obligations.when: Every lease-up and every year for the compliance period
obligations.who_reports: Property manager, reviewed by the owner
obligations.if_missed: Noncompliance reported to the IRS on Form 8823; credit recapture and investor remedies

obligations.what: Annual owner certification of continuing compliance and CHFA physical / file inspections
obligations.when: Annually, with inspections on CHFA's cycle
obligations.if_missed: Findings escalate to 8823 reporting; repeated findings affect the sponsor's standing in future QAP rounds

obligations.what: Investor and lender reporting — audited financials, operating budgets, reserve balances, debt-service coverage
obligations.when: Quarterly and annually through the 15-year compliance period
obligations.if_missed: Default under the partnership or loan agreements; loss of deferred developer fee

obligations.what: Year 15 and the extended-use period — investor exit, qualified-contract or right-of-first-refusal decisions, resyndication or preservation planning, and the Land Use Restriction Agreement that keeps rents restricted for the extended term (typically to year 30 or beyond)
obligations.when: Planning from about year 12; the extended-use period runs after the credits end
obligations.who_reports: Owner, with the investor and CHFA
obligations.if_missed: Affordability can be lost at the end of the extended-use period, or a preservation opportunity missed

obligations.what: Recording the deed restriction, covenant, or ground lease before the first sale
obligations.when: At or before the first closing
obligations.to_whom: County clerk and recorder; the funding source's compliance office
obligations.if_missed: The home sells unrestricted and the public subsidy is lost on that home

obligations.what: Buyer eligibility certification — income, asset, primary-residence, and first-time-buyer tests as the program requires
obligations.to_whom: Funding source (down-payment assistance, soft-second lender, Prop 123 or local program)
obligations.if_missed: Clawback of assistance; an ineligible buyer can void the restriction's enforceability

obligations.what: Annual owner-occupancy certification and monitoring of refinance, home-equity borrowing, and rental of the home
obligations.when: Annually for the term of the restriction
obligations.if_missed: Restriction violations that are hard to unwind after the fact; loss of the subsidy's purpose

obligations.what: Resale administration — formula price calculation, right of first refusal or purchase option, buyer qualification, and any subsidy recapture at sale
obligations.to_whom: Seller, buyer, and the funding source
obligations.if_missed: The home leaves the affordable stock at market price

obligations.what: Long-horizon stewardship — ground-lease renewals (CLTs typically 99 years), restriction terms of 30 to 99 years or perpetual, and the staffing and fees to administer them
obligations.when: For the life of the restriction
obligations.if_missed: Restrictions lapse when no one is left to enforce them

steps.why_it_matters: Lenders, equity investors, soft-debt sources, stewardship entities and buyer-assistance programs each expect a project to be at a certain level before they engage. Naming the level avoids approaching a funder too early, which usually gets a 'come back later'.

data_sources.label: Funding Sources
data_sources.what: Every Colorado tax credit, loan, grant and rental assistance program, with a finder that narrows them to the ones a project can use and shows their terms side by side

data_sources.label: CHFA Qualified Allocation Plan
data_sources.what: Scoring rules and policy priorities for the year

data_sources.label: CHFA portfolio of past awards
data_sources.what: Sponsor track record and regional allocation patterns

data_sources.label: Capital partner reference list
data_sources.what: 29 lenders, syndicators, and banks active in Colorado affordable housing

data_sources.label: Tax abatement and fee-waiver reference
data_sources.what: Property tax, PILOT, and fee waiver programs for 30 jurisdictions

steps.confidence_note: High on the framework — CHFA documents are public and explicit. Medium on the partner and abatement rosters, which depend on manual curation and should be re-verified annually.
watch_outs: CHFA's competitive 9% round draws roughly twice as many applications as it funds (14 of 32 in 2026, per CHFA's Round One applicant and award reports) — readiness alone does not guarantee an award.
The 4% bond cap can be exhausted partway through a year, deferring otherwise-ready projects to the next cycle.
Colorado state LIHTC, MIHTC, and Prop 123 dollars have their own readiness conventions that overlap but do not perfectly align with the federal LIHTC levels.
steps.does_not_tell_you: Whether CHFA will award credits to a specific project — the QAP is competitive and scoring outcomes depend on the full applicant pool each round — or, on the ownership track, whether a stewardship entity will take the home on and which resale convention the jurisdiction will accept.
steps.next_step: The current readiness level, on whichever track, determines what goes into the evidence package in Stage 7 — and the after-closing obligations above are what the evidence package should show the sponsor is prepared for.

steps.title: Evidence Package
steps.summary: Assemble a self-contained, public-data record for the jurisdiction-site pairing once it reaches Level 2 readiness.
steps.what_this_means: The evidence package is the public-data record assembled for a jurisdiction-site pairing once it reaches at least Level 2 readiness. It is a self-contained document of demographics, housing-stock context, rent triangulation across multiple sources (ACS, Zillow ZORI, Apartment List, HUD FMR), the AMI-tier gap analysis, the existing affordable inventory within and adjacent to the site, the funding-readiness summary, and the civic-capacity context.
steps.why_it_matters: A complete evidence package shortens every later conversation, with the jurisdiction, funders, neighbors and the project's own underwriters. It also keeps a dated record, so decisions can be revisited when the data refreshes.

data_sources.label: ACS demographic profile
data_sources.what: Population, income, tenure, rent, demographics

data_sources.label: HUD FMR & income limits
data_sources.what: Rent benchmarks and AMI tiers

data_sources.label: CHFA inventory
data_sources.what: Existing LIHTC supply

data_sources.label: ZORI & Apartment List rent series
data_sources.what: Market rent triangulation

data_sources.label: Local-resources directory
data_sources.what: Champions, advocates, agencies

steps.confidence_note: High on the underlying data. Medium on any forward-looking projection (rent growth, household growth) the package may include, which is always presented as a range, not a point estimate.
watch_outs: Rents from four sources will not agree. Report the spread.
Existing affordable inventory near a site can either support a new project (proven demand) or signal saturation (competing lease-up). The package distinguishes the two by AMI tier and unit type.
Funding-readiness figures change with each annual allocation cycle and should be dated.
steps.does_not_tell_you: Whether the project will be approved or funded. The package supports decisions; it does not make them.
steps.next_step: With the evidence package assembled, a specific next action becomes possible in Stage 8.

steps.title: Next Action
steps.summary: End the analysis with one named, dated next step.
steps.what_this_means: Every jurisdiction-site pairing that completes Stages 1-7 ends with a single named next action — a concrete, dated, public step that moves the project forward.
examples: Schedule a pre-application meeting with the jurisdiction's planning department
Submit a Letter of Intent to CHFA's pre-application process
Request a fee-waiver determination from the city manager
steps.why_it_matters: An analysis that ends in more analysis does not produce housing. Ending each pairing with a named action keeps the work tied to the goal: homes in service for households at 30-80% AMI.

data_sources.label: Reads from Stages 3, 5, and 6
data_sources.what: Procedural rather than data-driven

steps.confidence_note: High when the prior steps have been completed cleanly. Low when any prior step has been skipped — in which case the next action is to return to the skipped step rather than to advance.
watch_outs: A next action without an owner and a date is not a next action.
Some next actions are the responsibility of the jurisdiction rather than the developer; naming the responsible party matters.
If two cycles pass without progress on the named action, the pairing returns to Stage 4 for re-classification rather than continuing to age in the pipeline.
steps.next_step: Execute, document outcome, and re-enter at the appropriate prior step.

verification_questions.title: Ten questions to verify a jurisdiction locally
verification_questions.preface: Public data gets to a short list. These ten questions, asked of named local staff or partners, confirm whether a jurisdiction is ready for a project conversation.
questions: Does the jurisdiction have a current, adopted Housing Needs Assessment, and what AMI tiers does it call out as priority?
Is there site control or a credible path to site control on a specific parcel within the next 6-12 months?
Who is the named local champion on staff or council, and when was the last direct conversation with them?
What is the jurisdiction's recent track record with LIHTC awards, and is CHFA already familiar with the local sponsor pool?
Is bond cap available through DOLA or CHFA for a 4% deal, or is the realistic path a competitive 9% application?
Are LIHTC rents at the target AMI tier meaningfully below market rents in this place, and by how much?
Does the jurisdiction's zoning code permit the unit count and density required, or will a rezoning, variance, or PUD be required?
What is the housing authority's capacity, and have they committed to project-based vouchers, operating subsidy, or land contribution?
Has the community already absorbed comparable LIHTC inventory recently, and is there documented market depth for new units?
Are there active community-opposition signals — recent council votes, vocal HOAs, NIMBY pressure on adjacent projects — that would put approval at risk?

public_private_boundary.title: Public methodology, private deal work
public_private_boundary.body: Everything described above runs on data the public can read. The American Community Survey, HUD income limits and Fair Market Rents, CHFA's published LIHTC inventory and Qualified Allocation Plan, the Census Bureau's TIGER geographic files, and published municipal land inventories together cover every quantitative claim made on this page. What this site adds is joining those sources, checking them, dating them, and applying the same framework in every jurisdiction.
what_is_public: The eight-stage framework itself — steps, definitions, methodology
Classification criteria (A/B/C/D) and evidence types — without jurisdiction names attached
Confidence labels, watch-outs, data sources, vintages
Glossary, AMI dollar-anchor table, source list
what_stays_private: Specific jurisdiction A/B/C/D assignments used in any private planning process

public_private_boundary.boundary_rule: The public page describes the process. Private workspaces hold the outputs of applying that process to specific jurisdictions. A reader of this page should be able to understand how a jurisdiction would be classified, without seeing how any specific jurisdiction is currently classified by any particular party.

closing.title: Inspect, challenge, improve
closing.body: This methodology is educational. It is written for housing authorities, jurisdictions, funders, advocates and the public, and corrections are welcome. Data vintages and source documentation for every dataset referenced here are listed on the Data Health page. If a number on this site looks wrong, the fastest path to a correction is to check the relevant dataset's vintage there and email info@cohoanalytics.com with what you find.
